title: Motherhood shifts career advancement into a flexibility trade-off inside a global organization
source_unit: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11459, What Drives Child Penalties? Evidence from a Global Organization
geography: Headquarters-based professional staff at the World Bank Group, spanning employees from more than 190 countries; analysis period 1988-2024

observations.period: First six years after first childbirth; headquarters professional staff observed before and after childbirth

denominator.unit: final longitudinal sample: 1,617 mothers and 1,710 fathers

motherhood_earnings_penalty.value: mothers earn 3.1% below their counterfactual trajectory on average in the first six years after childbirth

promotion_gap.value: by year six, mothers have missed roughly one-quarter of a grade promotion relative to their counterfactual trajectory

performance_ratings.value: declines in performance ratings affecting annual salary increases are temporary and largely disappear within a few years

mechanism.value: the observed penalty is primarily an advancement penalty rather than a persistent measured-performance penalty

observations.method: Heterogeneity-robust staggered event-study difference-in-differences using variation in the timing of first childbirth among eventual parents, linked to administrative earnings, grades, performance, responsibilities, travel, work arrangements, and outputs.
observations.uncertainty: The study concerns highly skilled full-time professional staff in one global organization and estimates within-organization career trajectories; it does not establish population-wide earnings effects or identify every household-care mechanism.
observations.subgroup: Mothers, fathers, caregivers, professional employees, managers, organizations with promotion ladders, and households negotiating time and career investment.
observations.counterinterpretation: Observed sorting may reflect employee preferences, organizational constraints, caregiving needs, or job matching rather than an imposed penalty alone; the design estimates the post-birth trajectory, not a single causal actor’s intent.

observations.period: Post-childbirth allocation of responsibilities and outputs within the World Bank Group

denominator.unit: parents with linked project-responsibility observations for project initiation and supervision

leadership.value: mothers become substantially less likely to initiate new development projects and take on leadership responsibilities after childbirth; fathers show no comparable change

consultant_supervision.value: mothers are 32.5% less likely to supervise external consultants after childbirth in the reported estimate

output_quality.value: the study finds little robust evidence of changes in ex post project success, implementation speed, or research impact among realized outputs

allocation_mechanism.value: career penalties can arise because access to visible, promotion-enhancing responsibilities changes even when the quality of completed work does not materially fall

observations.method: Event-study estimates linked to project initiation, active project supervision, external-consultant supervision, ex-post project ratings, implementation delay, working-paper authorship, downloads, and research impact.
observations.uncertainty: Responsibility and output datasets cover different subsets and periods; quality measures capture realized outputs and do not observe every dimension of mentoring, relationship-building, or unrecorded work.
observations.subgroup: Women returning after childbirth, fathers, project leaders, consultants, teams, supervisors, and organizations that reward visibility and responsibility accumulation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Reducing travel or leadership assignments may be a rational response to caregiving constraints or a mutually agreed accommodation; the finding does not show that every assignment reduction is discriminatory or welfare-reducing.

observations.period: Post-childbirth job movement, travel intensity, and home-based-work sorting

denominator.unit: parents with information on the probability of work-related travel; other linked samples vary

travel.value: mothers reduce work-related travel more sharply than fathers after childbirth

internal_sorting.value: mothers become less likely to switch jobs and increasingly sort into positions with lower promotion potential, lower travel demands, and greater opportunities for home-based work

flexibility_tradeoff.value: motherhood penalties are larger in travel-intensive jobs and tend to be smaller in jobs that can be performed from home

work_control_mechanism.value: flexibility can reduce the immediate career penalty while also concentrating mothers in roles with weaker advancement prospects

observations.method: Event-study estimates combined with job-characteristic measures for promotion potential, travel intensity, home-based work, job switching, leave, schedules, and employee work arrangements.
observations.uncertainty: Conditional travel duration is available for 931 parents and home-based-work measures for 1,393; observed sorting does not establish whether organizations, employees, managers, or household constraints initiate each move.
observations.subgroup: Caregivers in travel-intensive and flexible jobs, dual-earner households, managers allocating assignments, remote-capable teams, and employees with different cultural and family contexts.
observations.counterinterpretation: Flexible or home-based roles may preserve employment, autonomy, and family stability even if they have lower promotion potential; advancement is not the only welfare-relevant outcome.

boundary: This record adds a within-organization mechanism linking parenthood to advancement, responsibility allocation, travel, job sorting, and flexibility. It is causal evidence for the studied World Bank professional-staff setting, not proof of a universal motherhood penalty, discriminatory intent, household welfare loss, or long-run labor-market effects across populations.
